title: From quadratic to fast
description:
Each of these has an obvious O(n²) solution. Write them faster; the tests include inputs of 100,000 elements, where O(n²) takes far too long.

```cpp
bool hasDuplicate(std::vector<int> values);                                  // O(n log n): sort a copy, compare neighbours
bool hasPairWithSum(const std::vector<int>& sorted, int target);             // O(n): two indexes moving towards each other
long long maxSubarraySum(const std::vector<int>& values);                    // O(n): the largest sum of a non-empty run of neighbours
std::size_t countBelow(const std::vector<int>& sorted, int limit);           // O(log n): how many values are < limit
```

- `hasPairWithSum` gets a vector sorted in ascending order and reports whether two **different positions** add up to `target`. Start one index at each end: if the sum is too small, move the left one right; too big, move the right one left.
- `maxSubarraySum` (Kadane's algorithm): walk once, keeping the best sum of a run that **ends here**: either this value alone, or this value added to the best run ending at the previous one. The answer is the largest of those. For an empty vector it returns 0.
- `countBelow` halves the search range each step (or uses `std::lower_bound`).
hints: For the pair sum, `lo` and `hi` together move at most n steps in total, because each step moves one of them inward.
In Kadane's algorithm, a run that has gone negative only drags down whatever comes next, so the best run ending at `i` either extends the previous one or starts fresh at `i`.
